title: Going deep first
objectives: Implement depth-first search recursively and with a stack.
Record pre-order and post-order, and count connected components

screens.title: Down one corridor
screens.prose: Explore from A like a maze. At each node, go to the first neighbour, alphabetically, that you have not visited. When none is left, step back to the node you came from and try again there.

state.caption: The graph from the last lesson

screens.question: Put the nodes in the order you first reach them.

hints.text: From A go to B, then keep going from B before you think about D.
From E, the first unvisited neighbour is G, not H.
A, B, E, G, C, D, F. At F you are stuck, so step back to D, C, G and E. E still has H.

feedback.correct: A, B, E, G, C, D, F, H.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep going from the newest node, and step back only when it has no unvisited neighbour.

byKey.D: You went to D straight after B. That finishes A's neighbours first, which is the BFS order. Here you keep going from B.
byKey.H: You went to H before G. From E, G comes first alphabetically; H waits until you step back.
byKey.C: C comes after G: you reach it from G, going deeper.

explain.text: You kept going from the newest node and backed up only at a dead end. This is **depth-first search**, or DFS. BFS gave A, B, D, E, C, F, G, H on the same graph.

screens.title: Where you back up
screens.prose: Walk the same dive again. Somewhere you reach a node whose neighbours are all visited.

state.caption: Visited so far: A, B, E, G, C, D

screens.question: Tap the first node where you get stuck and must step back.

hints.text: Where does the walk go from D?
D's neighbours are A, C and F.
From D the only unvisited neighbour is F. F's only neighbour, D, is visited, so F is a dead end.

feedback.correct: At F nothing new is left, so the search steps back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Continue the walk from D and find the first node with no unvisited neighbour.

byKey.H: H is a dead end too, but the walk reaches it last, after backing up from F to E.
byKey.D: D still has F unvisited, so the walk goes on to F first.

explain.text: From F the search steps back to D, C, G and E, each with nothing new. E still has H, so the dive continues there. That stepping back is **backtracking**, and a recursive call returning does it for free.

screens.title: Recursive DFS
screens.prose: Each call visits one node, then calls itself on each unvisited neighbour. When a call returns, you are back at the node before: the backtracking you just did.
screens.question: Complete `visit(u)` so that `dfs(adj, start)` returns the DFS order, neighbours in sorted order.

widget.starter:
def dfs(adj, start):
    seen = set()
    order = []

    def visit(u):
        ...

    visit(start)
    return order
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, including a single node, a triangle (a cycle), a disconnected graph and a directed graph. Neighbours are taken in sorted order, so each answer is a single list.

hints.text: `visit(u)` marks `u`, records it, then visits each neighbour not yet seen.
The walk from E chose G before H.
In `visit`: `seen.add(u)`, `order.append(u)`, then `for v in sorted(adj[u]): if v not in seen: visit(v)`.

feedback.correct: Mark, record, then recurse into each unvisited neighbour.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is a triangle. If it never finished, a node was visited twice: check `seen` before each call.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is a single node with no edges. The answer is `["A"]`.

explain.text: The `seen` set stops the search walking round a cycle. Each node is visited once and each edge read twice. So DFS is $O(V + E)$, like BFS; only the order differs.

screens.title: No memory of where you have been
screens.prose:
This version has no `seen` set.

```python
def dfs(adj, u, order):
    order.append(u)
    for v in sorted(adj[u]):
        dfs(adj, v, order)

dfs(tri, "A", [])
```

state.caption: A triangle: a cycle of three

screens.question: What happens on the triangle?

options.why: You expected it to stop once every node was seen. Nothing records that, so A calls B, B calls A, A calls B again.
Each call waits on the next, so frames pile up on the call stack. Python stops at about 1,000 frames and raises an error.
No call ever returns: the first neighbour of B is A, which starts the loop again.

hints.text: What does `dfs(tri, "B", order)` call first?
B's first neighbour is A.
A calls B, B calls A, A calls B: the calls never end. Each one adds a frame to the stack.

feedback.correct: The calls go round the cycle until Python's frame limit stops them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the calls: A's first neighbour is B, and B's is A.

byKey.ok: You expected the search to stop when every node was visited. With no `seen` set it never knows, so A and B call each other.
byKey.hang: You expected an endless hang. Recursion piles up frames, and Python raises `RecursionError` at about 1,000.

explain.text: Without `seen`, every cycle is walked round forever. A loop-based search would hang, but recursion fails fast with `RecursionError`. On a tree there is no cycle, so the bug can hide until real data arrives.

screens.title: A stack instead of recursion
screens.question: What is `order` at the end?

options.why: That is the recursive order. Here B and D are pushed in that order, and `pop` takes the last one pushed: D.
That is the BFS order. A stack takes the newest node, so the search still dives deep.

hints.text: After A, the stack holds B then D. Which does `pop` take?
`pop` takes the last item pushed.
D comes off first, then D's last neighbour F, then C, and so on. B is pushed first and popped last.

feedback.correct: Still depth first, but the largest neighbour first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `pop` takes the most recently pushed node.

explain.text: This is a valid depth-first order, mirrored: it explores the largest neighbour first. Pushing the neighbours in reverse sorted order makes the smallest come off first. Then the stack version matches the recursive one exactly.

screens.title: Match the recursive order
screens.prose: Write the stack version so that it returns exactly what the recursive `dfs` returns. Mark a node seen when you pop it, and skip it if it was seen already.

state.caption: Target: A, B, E, G, C, D, F, H

screens.question: Write `dfs_stack(adj, start)` with a list as the stack and no recursion.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each must equal the recursive `dfs` order exactly. Test 6 is a path of 5,000 nodes, deeper than Python's recursion limit.

hints.text: Push the neighbours so that the smallest is on top.
A node can be on the stack twice, as G is here.
Pop `u`; if seen, `continue`. Else mark it, record it, and push `sorted(adj[u], reverse=True)` that are not seen.

feedback.correct: Reverse-sorted pushes plus a skip on pop give the recursive order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: If you got A, D, F, ... the largest neighbour comes off first. Push `sorted(adj[u], reverse=True)`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is a square. If D appeared twice, skip a popped node that is already in `seen`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is a path of 5,000 nodes. A recursive helper hits the frame limit; keep it all in the loop.

explain.text: A node may sit on the stack twice, pushed by two neighbours; the skip on pop handles that. With marking on pop, the order matches the recursive one. The stack is an ordinary list, so 5,000 levels deep is no problem.

screens.title: When each call finishes
screens.prose: Now record each node when its call **finishes**, after all its neighbours are done. F finishes first: it has nothing left to explore.

state.caption: First reached: A, B, E, G, C, D, F, H

screens.question: Put the nodes in the order their calls finish.

hints.text: A call finishes only after every call it made has finished.
D finishes right after F, its last open branch.
F, D, C, G finish as the search backs up. Then H, then E, B and finally A.

feedback.correct: F, D, C, G, H, E, B, A.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A node finishes only after all the nodes it led to.

byKey.A: A's call is the first to start and the last to finish.
byKey.H: H finishes before E, because E's call made H's call.

explain.text: First-reached order is **pre-order**; finishing order is **post-order**. In post-order every node comes after all the nodes it led to. Lesson 5 uses exactly this to order tasks.

canvas.caption: Post-order: F, D, C, G, H, E, B, A

screens.title: Too deep for recursion
screens.prose: Python allows about 1,000 frames on its call stack, as you saw in Algorithmic Thinking. Your recursive `dfs` runs on a chain of 5,000 trades, each linked to the next.

state.caption: A chain: each call waits for the next

screens.question: What happens?

options.text: It works: the chain has no cycle
options.why: No cycle is needed. Each call waits for the next, so 5,000 frames are open at once, far over the limit.

options.text: It works after `sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6)`, which is always safe
options.why: Raising the limit lets Python's own C stack overflow instead, which can crash the interpreter. An explicit stack has no such limit.

hints.text: How many calls are open at once when the search reaches the far end?
Each call returns only after the next one does.
About 5,000 frames would be open at once. The limit is about 1,000, so Python stops with `RecursionError`.

feedback.correct: The depth of the search, not its size, breaks recursion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the calls that are open at the same moment.

explain.text: Recursion depth equals the length of the longest path the search follows. A chain or a long grid path easily passes 1,000. Use the stack version for big graphs.

screens.title: Counting the pieces
screens.prose: A graph may fall into several pieces, its **connected components**. Start a search from every node not yet seen; each new start is a new component.

state.caption: Two components: {A, B, D, E, F, H} and {C, G}

screens.question: Write `count_components(adj)` for an undirected graph.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on undirected graphs. They include an empty graph, nodes with no edges, a self-loop and a 3,000-node path.

hints.text: Loop over every node. Skip it if a previous search already reached it.
A search from A never reaches C or G, so a second start is needed. A node with no edges is a component by itself.
For each `s` not in `seen`: add 1, then run a stack DFS from `s` that marks everything it reaches.

feedback.correct: Each fresh start finds one whole component.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 has Z with no edges. It is a component on its own, so the answer is 2.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is the empty graph: no nodes, no components.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is a path of 3,000 nodes. A recursive search runs out of frames; use a stack.

explain.text: All the searches together touch each node and edge once, so counting is $O(V + E)$. The outer loop is what catches the pieces a single search misses. BFS would work just as well inside it.

screens.title: Rules that reference each other
screens.prose: A trading system's rules read other rules: `hedge` reads `delta`, and so on. A loop of rules can never be evaluated. In a directed graph, meeting a visited node is not enough: it must be on the **current** path.

state.caption: An arrow means "reads": two arrows reach spot, with no loop

screens.question: Write `has_cycle(rules)`: `True` if some rule depends on itself through a chain of reads.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Every rule is a key, and each list names the rules it reads. Return `True` or `False`.

hints.text: Give each rule three states: new, active (on the current path), done.
spot is reached twice, by delta and vega, yet there is no loop.
In `visit(u)`: mark it active. A neighbour that is active means a cycle. Visit new neighbours. Mark `u` done before returning.

feedback.correct: Only an edge back to an active rule is a cycle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is the drawing: spot is reached twice, with no loop. A plain `seen` set calls that a cycle; track the current path instead.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has `limit` reading itself: a cycle of one rule.
byKey.test-5: Test 5's loop c → d → e → c is not reachable from a. Start a search from every rule.

explain.text: In the drawing, vega reaches spot after delta has finished with it, so spot is done, not active. A cycle shows up only as an edge back into the current path. The same three states detect a cycle among tasks in lesson 5.

ideas: Depth-first search keeps going from the newest node and backs up at dead ends. Recursion does the backing up; an explicit stack does the same in a loop.
Both versions need a `seen` set. To match the recursive order, push neighbours in reverse sorted order and skip nodes already seen when popped.
Pre-order records a node when first reached, post-order when its call finishes. Recursion depth can pass Python's limit of about 1,000 frames on long paths.

formula.name: DFS cost
formula.note: The same as BFS: each node once, each edge once from each end.

summary.trap: Without a `seen` set, DFS walks round every cycle until Python raises `RecursionError`.

quiz.prose: A holdings graph links each firm to the firms it owns shares in, treated as undirected. You need every firm connected to Firm X through any chain.
quiz.question: Which search gives you that set?

options.text: Either BFS or DFS from X
Only BFS, because it goes level by level
options.why: BFS gives the levels, but any search that marks seen nodes reaches the same component.

options.text: Only DFS, because it follows chains
options.why: DFS follows chains, but BFS reaches exactly the same firms, in a different order.

feedback.correct: Both reach X's whole connected component.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which firms each search can reach.

explain.text: BFS and DFS differ in order, not in what they reach. Both visit X's connected component and nothing else.

quiz.question: How many connected components does this graph have?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Group the nodes joined by paths, and count every group.

byKey.edges: You counted only groups with edges. A node with no edges is a component by itself.
byKey.nodes: You counted every node. 1 and 2 are joined, and so are 4 and 5.

explain.text: Searches start from 1, 3, 4 and 6; 2 and 5 are already seen when their turn comes. Four starts, four components.

quiz.prose: DFS runs on an undirected tree of 10 nodes. Ignore the edge back to the node a call came from.
quiz.question: How many times does it meet an already-visited node?

widget.label: Times
widget.accept: 0: a tree has no cycles, so no edge leads back to a visited node except the parent edge.

feedback.correct: A tree has no cycle, so nothing leads back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what an edge back to a visited node would mean.

byKey.edges: 9 is the number of edges. Each leads to a new node; only the parent edge looks back, and you ignore it.

explain.text: An edge to a visited node other than the parent would close a cycle. A tree has none, so the answer is 0. That is also how DFS tests whether an undirected graph is a tree.

quiz.prose: A tree: R has children S and T, and S has one child, U. DFS starts at R and takes children in that order.
quiz.question: What is the post-order?

options.why: That is the pre-order: nodes as they are first reached. Post-order records each when its call finishes.
That reverses the pre-order. A node finishes after its children, so R comes last.
That is level by level, the BFS order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Record each node only when all its children are done.

explain.text: U has no children, so it finishes first; then S. T finishes next, and R last. Every node comes after its descendants.
